payload.body: A Wiener filter is a human-made optimal linear filter that estimates a desired signal from noisy observations by minimizing the mean-squared error between the estimate and the target. Parameters: (1) the signal and noise power spectral densities S_x(f), S_n(f) — the frequency-domain solution is H(f) = S_x(f) / (S_x(f) + S_n(f)), so the a priori signal-to-noise ratio profile sets the gain at each frequency; (2) the filter structure — a frequency-domain transfer function, or a time-domain tap set solved from the Wiener–Hopf normal equations (FIR or IIR realization); (3) the statistical assumptions — joint second-order stationarity, within which the Wiener solution is the best LINEAR estimator (optimal within the linear class, not necessarily overall); (4) the adaptation regime — a fixed steady-state design, or an adaptive approximation (LMS/RLS) tracking non-stationary spectra. Persistence mechanism: persists as the canonical solution of the linear minimum-mean-squared-error problem in signal-processing textbooks, as a standard stage in speech-enhancement and audio-deconvolution toolchains, in communications receiver filtering and geophysical Wiener deconvolution, and as the limit that Kalman filtering generalizes in the time domain. [formal: filtrum optimum | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

payload.body: A butterworth-filter is a human-made filter design — the classic maximally-flat (zero-ripple) magnitude response — defined by its parameters: (1) order N, the number of pole pairs, fixing roll-off beyond cutoff at 20N dB/decade; (2) cutoff frequency wc, where the gain falls to 1/sqrt(2) (-3 dB); (3) the prototype magnitude |H(jw)| = 1/sqrt(1 + (w/wc)^(2N)), whose N poles lie on a left-half s-plane semicircle (for the digital IIR realization, mapped inside the unit circle in the z-plane by the bilinear transform). It persists as the named reference design in every DSP textbook and filter-design toolkit: the standard analog prototype from which digital IIR filters are derived by bilinear transform or impulse invariance, and the flatness yardstick against which Chebyshev and elliptic designs are compared. [formal: filtrum butterworthianum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.75]

payload.body: An objective metric that quantifies the perceptual difference between two utterances by computing the root-mean-square deviation of their mel-cepstral coefficient vectors in the mel-frequency domain. Parameters: reference_coefficients (finite sequence of real-valued mel-cepstral coefficients), comparison_coefficients (finite sequence of mel-cepstral coefficients of matching length and dimension), coefficient_count (positive integer specifying the number of cepstral coefficients per frame). Persistence: specified in ITU-T P.56 and ETSI TS 103 197 speech quality standards, implemented in open-source evaluation toolkits (HTS toolkit, WORLD vocoder utilities, OpenSMILE), and published in peer-reviewed audio engineering literature including ICASSP and SLT proceedings. Displayed as a single non-negative real value expressed in mel-scale distance units, where higher values indicate greater perceptual distortion.

payload.body: A vocoder that synthesizes speech by modeling and resynthesizing the vocal tract's formant frequencies — the resonant peaks of the speech spectrum. Parameters: input audio signal, formant detection algorithm (e.g., linear prediction analysis), formant frequency tracks, bandwidth parameters, and amplitude envelopes for each formant band. Persistence mechanism: software implementation of the formant analysis-synthesis pipeline, typically realized through digital signal processing algorithms that extract formant parameters from speech and reconstruct them via excitation-source filtering. The output preserves the perceptual qualities of voiced speech while enabling pitch and duration control independent of the original source. [formal: formant-vocoder | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Butterworth filter is a human-made signal-processing filter type designed to have a maximally flat magnitude response in the passband, with no ripples. Parameters: (1) filter order N (determines roll-off steepness at -20N dB/decade in the stopband), (2) cutoff frequency fc (the -3 dB point where response drops to 1/√2 of passband gain), (3) filter type — low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or band-stop, (4) passband ripple tolerance (zero by design — the Butterworth characteristic is maximally flat). The transfer function has all poles evenly spaced on a semicircle in the left half of the s-plane (analog) or mapped to the z-plane (digital). Unlike Chebyshev or elliptic filters, it sacrifices roll-off steepness for a monotonic, ripple-free response. Persistence mechanism: stored as coefficient arrays in DSP libraries, filter-design toolkits (MATLAB, SciPy, GNU Radio), and embedded audio processing systems; persists through textbook implementations, standardized filter-design tables, and audio engineering practice where flat passband response is prioritized over selectivity. [formal: butterworthianum filtrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: Falsifiability is a human-made epistemological criterion that demarcates scientific claims from non-scientific ones by requiring that every scientific theory admit of at least one conceivable observation that could count against it. A Butterworth filter is a human-made analog or digital filter design characterized by maximally flat frequency response in the passband, with no ripples. Parameters: (1) filter order N (determines rolloff steepness of 20·N dB/decade), (2) cutoff frequency fc (3 dB point where response drops), (3) passband ripple (zero by design), (4) stopband attenuation profile. A Butterworth filter of order N has all poles placed on a semicircle in the left half of the s-plane at equal angular intervals, yielding the flat magnitude response |H(f)|² = 1/(1+(f/fc)^(2N)). Persistence mechanism: persists through filter design textbooks (Sedra/Smith, Oppenheim), standard electronic component catalogs, SPICE model libraries, DSP implementation toolkits (MATLAB's filter design, SciPy's scipy.signal.butter), and analog circuit design handbooks. [formal: butterworth | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The master of this servant is speech-quality assessment; pointing it at speech-recognition is master-attribution error. STRIKE.

payload.scope: A statistical model for binary outcome data that uses the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution as its link function, built for parameter estimation and hypothesis testing in regression contexts.

payload.scope: A statistical model for binary outcome data that uses the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution as its link function, built for parameter estimation and hypothesis testing in regression contexts.

payload.body: A probit-model is a regression technique for binary dependent variables where the latent variable y* is modeled as a linear combination of predictors (y* = Xβ + ε) with ε ~ N(0,1), and the observed binary outcome y equals 1 when y* > 0 and 0 otherwise. The probability P(y=1|x) = Φ(Xβ) where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (the probit link). Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood. The model persists through statistical software implementations (R's glm family=binomial(link='probit'), Python's statsmodels Probit, Stata's probit) and its formal statement in econometric and biostatistical textbooks. payload.body: An information-theoretic criterion for statistical model selection, defined by the formula AIC = 2k − 2ln(L), where k is the number of estimated parameters in the model and L is the maximized likelihood. The criterion estimates the relative information loss when a given model is used to represent the process that generated the data; lower AIC values indicate less estimated loss. It balances goodness-of-fit (via log-likelihood) against model complexity (via the penalty term 2k), automating the trade-off between underfitting and overfitting. Computed by evaluating each candidate model's log-likelihood at its maximum-likelihood estimates, counting its free parameters, and applying the formula. Published by Hirotugu Akaike in 1974 as derived from Kullback–Leibler divergence, it persists through statistical textbooks, software implementations (R, Python, MATLAB), and research practice across disciplines including econometrics, ecology, signal processing, and machine learning. [formal: AIC | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.10]

payload.body: A statistical technique that combines predictions from multiple candidate models by computing a weighted average, rather than selecting a single best model. Given m candidate models with predictions f_i(x) and non-negative weights w_i summing to 1, the averaged prediction at input x is Σ_{i=1}^{m} w_i · f_i(x). The weights are typically derived from a model selection criterion such as AIC: w_i = exp(−Δ_i / 2) / Σ_j exp(−Δ_j / 2), where Δ_i is the difference between model i's AIC and the minimum AIC across all candidates. Model averaging reduces selection uncertainty and often produces more accurate predictions than any individual model, especially when no single model is clearly superior. Computed by evaluating each candidate model, deriving weights from a criterion, and forming the weighted sum. Established in statistical practice through Burnham and Anderson (2002) and earlier Bayesian model averaging (Raftery et al., 1997), it persists through statistical textbooks, software packages (R's MuMIn, AICcmodavg), and research practice across ecology, econometrics, climate science, and machine learning. payload.body: Mel-cepstral distortion (MCD) is an objective metric that approximates the perceptual spectral difference between a reference utterance and a processed or synthesized utterance by comparing their mel-frequency cepstral coefficient vectors frame by frame. For each aligned frame pair, with c_i the processed-utterance coefficients and r_i the reference coefficients (typically i = 1..L with L = 12 or 13; the 0th coefficient c_0, overall level, is excluded or weighted), MCD(frame) = 10·log10( sqrt( sum_i (c_i - r_i)^2 / sum_i r_i^2 ) ) dB, and the reported value is the average over the overlapping frames. Parameters: (1) coefficient order range L, (2) c_0 treatment (excluded or weighted), (3) frame alignment and overlap interval. Persistence: standardized objective metric for TTS and speech-enhancement evaluation in the ITU-T P.56 lineage, implemented in the HTS toolkit, WORLD vocoder utilities, and OpenSMILE, and routinely reported in dB in the ICASSP and SLT speech-synthesis literature. [formal: distortio cepstralis mel | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A statistical estimator is a rule mapping a sample of observed data (random variables) to an estimate of an unknown quantity — a parameter of, or functional of, the data-generating distribution; a point estimator maps to a single value, an interval estimator to a set with a coverage level. Its parameters are the sample, the target estimand, and the assumed sampling distribution. It persists because its performance is formally evaluable against the sampling distribution — bias, variance, mean squared error, consistency, asymptotic normality, sufficiency, efficiency — which makes it the unit of comparison in estimation theory: the theorems of the discipline (Cramér–Rao bound, Lehmann–Scheffé, asymptotics of maximum-likelihood estimation) are stated about estimators as a class, and specific estimators (maximum likelihood, minimum-variance unbiased, Bayes, method of moments) are named instances of this kind.

payload.scope: A human-made family of functions in probability theory and information theory that quantify the difference between two probability distributions, built to persist as a mathematical framework for comparing statistical models.

payload.body: A statistical divergence is a mathematical function D[P||Q] that takes two probability distributions P and Q over the same sample space and returns a non-negative real number measuring how dissimilar they are, with D[P||Q]=0 if and only if P=Q almost everywhere; it is parameterized by a generating functional or integral form (e.g. f-divergence via a convex function f, R\'enyi divergence via a real parameter α, Tsallis divergence via a real parameter q), and it persists as an abstracted class of functionals on the space of probability measures, distinguished by properties such as convexity, triangle inequality failure, and information-geometric monotonicity (Law 6, trailer).

payload.name: f-divergence
payload.scope: A human-made family of statistical divergences parameterized by a convex function f, built to persist as a unifying framework in information theory that includes KL-divergence, Hellinger distance, and χ²-divergence as special cases.

payload.name: f-divergence
payload.scope: A human-made family of statistical divergences parameterized by a convex function f, built to persist as a unifying framework in information theory that includes KL-divergence, Hellinger distance, and χ²-divergence as special cases.

payload.body: An f-divergence is a statistical divergence D_f[P||Q] between two probability distributions P and Q over the same sample space, defined as the expectation E_Q[f(dP/dQ)] where f is a fixed strictly convex function with f(1)=0 and dP/dQ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of P with respect to Q; specific choices of f yield specific divergences — f(t)=t log t gives KL-divergence, f(t)=(√t-1)² gives Hellinger distance, f(t)=(t-1)² gives χ²-divergence — and all f-divergences share the data-processing inequality: for any stochastic map T, D_f[P∘T⁻¹ || Q∘T⁻¹] ≤ D_f[P||Q], with persistence grounded in the convexity of f and the integral structure of probability measures (Law 6, trailer).

payload.name: state-space-model
payload.scope: A human-made mathematical representation of a physical or abstract system as a set of first-order differential or difference equations relating state variables, inputs, and outputs, built to persist as the standard formalism for modeling dynamic systems in engineering and control theory.

payload.name: state-space-model
payload.scope: A human-made mathematical representation of a physical or abstract system as a set of first-order differential or difference equations relating state variables, inputs, and outputs, built to persist as the standard formalism for modeling dynamic systems in engineering and control theory.

payload.body: A state-space model is a mathematical representation of a system as a set of first-order evolution equations: ẋ = f(x, u, t) for the state dynamics (where x is the state vector, u is the input vector, and f maps states and inputs to state derivatives) and y = h(x, u, t) for the output equation (where y is the output vector and h maps states and inputs to outputs), with persistence grounded in the state-variable formalism that reduces higher-order differential equations to coupled first-order form, enabling analysis of multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems, stability via eigenvalues of the Jacobian ∂f/∂x, and optimal estimation via recursive algorithms such as the Kalman filter (Law 6, trailer).

Log-likelihood is the logarithm of the likelihood function L(theta|x) = P(x|theta). Its computation requires observed data, a statistical model, parameters, and a logarithm — the note's own chain admits as much ('requires the likelihood function which itself depends on probability distributions'). KL divergence (D_KL(P||Q) = E_P[log P/Q]) is a separate quantity comparing two distributions; it plays no role in forming, computing, or using log-likelihood, which predates and operates independently of it (MLE, MAP, and likelihood-ratio tests all work without KL). Remove the KL-divergence construct and log-likelihood keeps operating exactly as before. The note never actually shows the removal's consequence for the from-end — it only says KL is 'the canonical divergence between distributions that log-likelihood evaluates,' which is neither true nor a dependency. Coherent claim, factually wrong: STRIKE.
